title: Agent-based modeling and simulation for an order-to-cash process using netlogo
contribution: A CMU ISR/CASOS technical report with Carley and Dow's Wassick. It builds a NetLogo agent-based model of a simplified Dow order-to-cash process and uses replicated sweeps to locate staffing bottlenecks. Staffing is searched one role at a time, and the authors expect full enumeration to change the optimum.
problem_entry: Order fulfilment in an order-to-cash process with many actors is hard to predict, and the authors hold that the process resists mathematical equations. They therefore use agent-based simulation for what-if analysis of a simplified Dow process (pp. 7-8).
key_idea: A NetLogo 5.3.1 model with people, unit and information agents. Settings cover queue discipline, initial efficiency with learning rewards, routing by availability or by expertise, and random errors that cause rework or return (pp. 9-14).
assumptions: People are modeled generically; the plant is 100% efficient and the other agents 90%; the error rate is 10%; inventory never runs out. Some agent actions were changed to reproduce the company's results. Face validation is named, but no validation data are shown (pp. 7-9, 13-15).
proof_devices: n/a (no proofs); replicated sweeps with 10 runs per test case (Tables 2-5, pp. 15-17)
two-sample t-test on initial training levels (Table 6, p. 24)
experiments: A sweep of 10-300 orders finds the customer representative to be the bottleneck (pp. 19-20). Two representatives raise performance from 22% to 47%, and a second transportation specialist cuts the time per order by about 13% (p. 28). Training is not significant (p = 0.636 and 0.0921, p. 24). Hiring is recommended without a test (pp. 24, 28).
positioning: Five agent-based supply-chain studies are summarized as inputs to the model, without critique (pp. 8-9).
writing: Plain report style. Each experiment has a table of independent and dependent variables with its replication count (Tables 2-5, pp. 15-17).
limits_future: The process is simplified because of time constraints (p. 8). The authors expect the optimum to differ under full enumeration of agents per role, and plan to port the model from NetLogo to C or C++ to make it larger (p. 28).

method_links.note: Weak, since his role is not stated. A simulator with integer staffing decisions (1-5 agents in each of four roles) is searched one role at a time. The remedy named is a faster code, not an algebraic surrogate or a derivative-free search.

transferable: Locate bottlenecks by tracking each agent's processing time as the load rises. After relieving one, measure again, because the next bottleneck appears elsewhere (pp. 19-27).
Give every intervention you compare the same replications and the same significance test before ranking them. Here training was tested and hiring was not (pp. 24, 28).
coauthors: John Villarraga, Kathleen M. Carley, John Wassick (Dow)

quotes.text: Some of their actions have been modified with the purpose of increasing the complexity of the model so as to obtain results similar to the ones provided by the company.

However, we theorized that the optimal number of agents for the simulation will differ from our current results, if we had the computational speed to conduct an experiment testing every possible combination of agents in each role.

title: Evaluation and demonstration of commercialization potential of CCSI tools within gPROMS advanced simulation platform
contribution: PSE's DOE final report on commercializing CCSI tools in gPROMS. ALAMO ranks first (69 of 100), and PSE's prototypes show its limits: phase changes, more inputs, and a physically reduced model that does better. Sahinidis's signed brochure states ALAMO's aims (simplest models a person can check for physical sense, few data points, constrained regression, adaptive sampling) and the business case for bundling it with BARON.
problem_entry: Which CCSI tools could PSE commercialize inside gPROMS, and by what technical path (pp. 4, 9)? Four fast-track tools were assessed and nine more screened.
key_idea: A stage-gate assessment: workshops, prototypes, SWOTs, screening, integration requirements, stakeholder feedback, and a 1-10 score on ten criteria with a cut-off of 50. ALAMO scores 69, ranks first, and is to be built into gPROMS Global System Analysis without external dependencies (pp. 12-32, 48-56).
assumptions: The criteria are PSE's own and include platform alignment (p. 50). DFO was dropped as off-strategy (p. 27), and tools depending on GAMS/BARON or GAMS were judged unattractive (pp. 28-29). PSE's SWOT lists adaptive sampling as not available yet (p. 24).
experiments: PSE's prototypes: the steam-property surrogate fails across phase changes (p. 14); the tubular-reactor surrogate is less accurate than a physically reduced CSTR model and shows the wrong trend at high composition (pp. 15-16); the ASU surrogate loses accuracy from two to five inputs (pp. 46-47). Results are in figures only; the text gives no error metrics.
positioning: His brochure says ALAMO's deterministic optimization often finds better models than Eureqa's genetic search, and that constrained regression is unique to ALAMO, without a benchmark (pp. 80-81). PSE repeats the first claim and adds over short time spans (p. 56).
writing: The brochure is in vendor voice: BARON is currently considered the best global MINLP solver, and feedback is very positive, with the installer and GUI criticism stated beside it (pp. 80-81).
limits_future: Phase 2 was unsuccessful and no licence was concluded (pp. 4, 10). Limits listed in the brochure: no installer, GUI or detailed manual; long run times that need trials of options; the GAMS/BARON and MATLAB/SNOBFIT requirements. Plans: defaults that work for most users, and full symbolic regression by deterministic optimization (pp. 80-81).

method_links.note: In his voice: the simplest model, so people can confirm its physical correctness; minimal data points; constrained regression; adaptive sampling from a large dataset. Symbolic regression by deterministic optimization is planned, and the surrogates are meant to support deterministic superstructure optimization.

Third-party view: PSE marks adaptive sampling as not available yet, while the brochure describes it as provided. PSE's tests show accuracy falling with more inputs and a physically reduced model beating the fitted basis.
ALAMO is powered by BARON, and the bundle is the claimed competitive edge. For a commercial partner, the closed dependency was a reason to drop tools or to ask for its removal.
Firm voice: comparative claims against Eureqa and all other regression software, made without a benchmark (Inner Tension 3).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: version, build and the paper to cite in every run log
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The ALAMO 2016.2.23 banner prints version and build and asks users to cite Cozad, Sahinidis and Miller 2014. The BARON 17.4.1 log does the same (S112 p. 10).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: published algorithm, proprietary engine as the moat
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: ALAMO's technology is published, but its subproblems need a global MINLP solver. Bundling it with BARON, owned by TOF, gives an edge over any competitor that takes a similar approach. The source code is not available through CCSI.

transferable: Before adopting or integrating a surrogate tool, test it against a physically reduced model of the same unit, on a case with phase changes and a case with more inputs, to see where a fitted basis stops working (pp. 14-16, 46-47).
In a tool's own description, list its concrete current limits (installer, GUI, manual length, run time, dependencies) next to its advantages (p. 81).
coauthors: Adekola Lawal, Pieter Schmal, Alfredo Ramos, Debangsu Bhattacharyya, David Mebane, Ananya Chowdhury, Xiaohui Liu, Stefan Bellinghausen (PI Alejandro Cano, PSE)

quotes.text: ALAMO returns the simplest regression model possible that fits the data well. As a result, humans can inspect ALAMO’s models and confirm the physical correctness of these models before using them.

title: Announcement: Howard Rosenbrock Prize 2017
contribution: Editor-in-chief's announcement of the 2017 Rosenbrock Prize of Optimization and Engineering, won by Le Thi and Pham Dinh for DCA for image restoration via a Markov random field model, with the committee's citation quoted.
problem_entry: n/a (announcement): the annual $500 prize, sponsored by Springer, for the best OPTE paper of the previous year (p. 1).
key_idea: n/a: the winners; the committee (Kwon, Epelman, Ohsaki); and the committee's citation, which praises DCA's finite termination and local-optimality guarantee over metaheuristics and graph-cut methods (pp. 1-2).
positioning: Lists past winners (Hicken; Simon and Ulbrich; Kim and Wright) and ties the prize to Rosenbrock's bridging of optimization and engineering, which is OPTE's main focus (pp. 1-2).
writing: Announcement format: his first-person opening and closing invitation. The research judgement is the committee's quoted citation (pp. 1-2).
limits_future: n/a: closes by inviting submissions at the interface of engineering and optimization (p. 2).

quotes.text: As the editor-in-chief of Optimization and Engineering (OPTE), I am delighted to announce the 2017 Rosenbrock Prize.
OPTE publishes high-quality articles at the interfaces between engineering and optimization.

title: Optimization of circuitry arrangements for heat exchangers using derivative-free optimization
contribution: Formulates refrigerant-circuitry design as a binary problem over an undirected adjacency matrix with explicit manufacturing constraints. Five DFO solvers are benchmarked on 17 simulated coils, with complete constraint-programming enumeration as ground truth for the five smallest. TOMLAB's DIRECT variants do best.
problem_entry: Circuitries are chosen by experience and enumerated simulation. N! designs, infeasible GA offspring and knowledge-based operators that are hard to define call for a systematic method that a manufacturing engineer can apply to a given coil (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: (t^2-t)/2 binaries over the upper triangle of the adjacency matrix (630 instead of 1,296 for 36 tubes), with inlet and outlet left free. Constraints: fixed far-end pairs, at most two connections per tube, no cycles. CoilDesigner is a black box; five DFO solvers are run, feasibility is checked before each simulation, and the capacity floor is a quadratic penalty (pp. 4-10).
assumptions: Geometry and inlet conditions are fixed, and other manufacturing rules are left out for simplicity. Inlet/outlet choice is assumed to matter little, on the basis of unreported experiments. The simulator is treated as deterministic (pp. 3-5, 8, 11).
proof_devices: n/a (no proofs); ground truth by complete enumeration of feasible circuitries with the Choco constraint-programming solver for 4-12 tubes (pp. 10-11, 16)
experiments: 17 coils of 4-36 tubes, with 2,500 evaluations and 86,400 s per run. glcDirect and glcSolve are optimal or within 0.05-0.15% where verified (the five smallest coils). CMAES, MIDACO and NOMAD fail on large coils. The run counts of the stochastic solvers are not stated (pp. 10-19).
positioning: Fills a gap: no systematic comparison of mixed-integer constrained DFO solvers on industrial problems existed. Extends the 2013 box-bounded comparison and picks CMAES from it (pp. 3, 9).
writing: A twofold aim in the abstract and contributions named in the introduction. Per-instance tables mark failures with dashes and give geometric means (pp. 1, 3, 13-19).
limits_future: Claims optimal or near-optimal designs on all instances, though only five were verified (p. 16). Future work: other metrics and other design parameters (p. 20).

method_links.note: Existing implementations are benchmarked on an industrial problem before any method of the authors' own: equal budgets, solver choice from the earlier benchmark, exact ground truth for small instances, failures shown per instance.

The objective is a black box, so ground truth comes from complete enumeration and only for 4-12 tubes. For 14-36 tubes, near-optimal means the best any solver found. The stochastic solvers apparently ran once each, so there is no median or best-run reporting.

The feasibility rules are written out and enforced before each simulation; only Q and dP stay black-box. No surrogate is considered despite the discrete decisions (step 1). At 36 tubes there are 630 binary inputs, beyond ALAMO's input range.

transferable: Encode a connection design as the upper triangle of an undirected adjacency matrix. When direction matters little, drop it and recover it afterwards by enumerating inlet/outlet choices, which halves the binaries; show the evidence that direction matters little (pp. 4-5, 10).
Write feasibility rules as explicit constraints and screen candidates before calling the simulator, so solvers that use penalties waste no simulations on infeasible points (p. 10).
Score black-box solvers on small instances for which a constraint-programming solver has enumerated every feasible design (pp. 10-11, 16).
Report the best value, time and evaluations per instance, mark runs without a feasible point, and add geometric means (pp. 13-19).
coauthors: Nikolaos Ploskas, Christopher Laughman, Arvind U. Raghunathan (MERL)

quotes.text: We also use constraint programming methods to verify the results of the DFO methods for small heat exchangers.
Results showed that TOMLAB/glcDirect and TOMLAB/glcSolve can find optimal or near-optimal refrigerant circuitry designs on all instances.

title: A machine learning approach to correlation development applied to fin-tube bundle heat exchangers
contribution: Builds fin-tube bundle correlations with ALAMO best-subset regression over public experiments plus adaptively sampled CFD points. Validation RMSE falls from 28% to 15% for Eu and from 33% to 25% for Nu. At a weight-optimization optimum, the error stays as large as that of the Escoa correlation.
problem_entry: Offshore waste-heat recovery units need accurate correlations with an extended validity range (tube diameters near 10 mm). Direct CFD optimization is too costly, and published correlations are narrow or rest on scattered data (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: ALAMO 2018.4.3 starts from 108 filtered experimental points and picks the basis subset by BIC, solved with BARON. CFD points are added where the model is most inconsistent. Log-transformed outputs and velocity give multiplicative correlations (pp. 3-5).
assumptions: A box design space; a 30-degree layout, with corrections of up to 5% and 9%; tube rows ignored. Periodic RANS CFD with Spalart-Allmaras and constant properties. The case study assumes a constant wall temperature and real-valued tube rows. Accuracy is bounded by that of the CFD model (pp. 3-6, 13).
proof_devices: n/a (no proofs); scaling argument for why the optimizer drives the tube diameter to its lower bound (pp. 8-9)
experiments: On a hold-out of 30 LHS CFD runs, Eu R2 rises from 0.75 to 0.94 (RMSE 28% to 15%) and Nu R2 from 0.70 to 0.76 (RMSE 33% to 25%) (Table 4, p. 7). At the optimum, CFD shows Eu off by +48% and +72% (Table 5, p. 9). The optimizer is fmincon SQP with 100 random starts (p. 6). No non-adaptive arm of equal size is run.
positioning: Presented as a contrast to fully connected ANN, SVR and RBNN heat-exchanger models, whose structure is less restricted. Benchmarked against the Holfeld, Escoa and PFR correlations (pp. 2, 7, 13).
writing: The hypothesis is stated as such and the novelty is given in three bullets (p. 2). The abstract reports the shortfall at the optimum (p. 1).
limits_future: The Nusselt number is the harder output, and the error at the optimum is as large as Escoa's. Dataset size limits how nonlinear the model can be. Future work: larger datasets from LHS plus adaptive sampling, and experiments on untested geometries such as the case-study optimum (pp. 1, 7, 13).

method_links.note: Best-subset selection by BIC, solved with BARON; a readable multiplicative form; trends read against CFD and physics; error-maximization sampling.
The surrogate is optimized by local SQP from 100 random starts, said to ensure a global optimum, instead of by a deterministic global solver (step 7). This also goes against Heuristic 7.
A hold-out of 30 Latin-hypercube CFD runs is never used in fitting, the optimum is checked by independent CFD, and the reference correlations are scored on the same hold-out.

transferable: Seed a correlation with filtered public experiments, add simulator points where the fitted model is most inconsistent, and keep a separate Latin-hypercube set of simulator runs for validation only (pp. 3-5).
Log-transform the outputs and any input with a known logarithmic effect, so the fitted correlation is multiplicative and reads as a base term times correction factors (p. 5).
Check a surrogate-based optimum by running the full simulator at the optimum and at one-at-a-time perturbations around it, judging the trends as well as the error at the point (pp. 9-13).
When pooling literature data, map them to one configuration with a correction derived from an existing correlation, and report the largest correction applied (p. 4).
coauthors: Karl Lindqvist, Zachary T. Wilson, Erling Næss

quotes.text: The quantitative error of predicted heat transfer and pressure drop coefficients at the case study optimum, however, was as large as those of the Escoa correlations.
The optimization was repeated 100 times for a given case, using random starting points within the design space, to ensure that a global, feasible optimum point was reached.

title: BARON user manual
contribution: BARON user manual v. 17.4.1 (April 2017; the index says 2018). It defines BARON as branch and bound plus range reduction under finite-bound assumptions and documents every reduction and relaxation device as a switch with a default. Its termination statuses separate solved within tolerances from heuristic results and from results with missing bounds.
problem_entry: n/a (manual): global solution of algebraic NLPs and MINLPs, with guarantees under fairly general assumptions, including finite bounds on nonlinear expressions (p. 2).
key_idea: Branch and bound with constraint propagation and duality-based range reduction. Five reduction switches are on by default, with probing decided automatically. Relaxations are LP/MIP with outer approximation. Further features: the k best or all solutions from one tree, a multistart mode, IIS search and complementarity detection (pp. 2, 16-20, 23-24).
assumptions: Functions must be algebraic and explicit (exp, ln, x^α, β^x; no trigonometric functions; the same list as in 2000). Finite bounds must be supplied or inferred, otherwise there is no global guarantee. Defaults: EpsA 1e-6, EpsR 1e-4, MaxTime 1000 s (pp. 3, 20-22).
proof_devices: n/a (manual); termination test |U-L| <= epsA or <= epsR|L| (pp. 20-21)
status vocabulary separating solved within tolerances, heuristic termination, missing bounds and numerical sensitivity (pp. 12-14)
experiments: none (worked examples only: gear-train log pp. 9-11, the 14 solutions of the PUMA robot system pp. 16-18, an IIS p. 19)
positioning: A bibliography of 41 BARON-related publications (1995-2017), declared to describe the algorithms implemented; the 1996 BARON note is listed twice (pp. 28-31).
writing: Firm voice. Every option appears with its range and default, and each termination message is paired with the user's next action (pp. 12-13, 20-28).
limits_future: Missing bounds void the guarantee, and the printed bounds may be invalid. Numerically sensitive results are only likely correct. DeltaTerm may make runs nondeterministic. IIS search and NumSol slow the search. The demo is size-limited (pp. 2-3, 12-13, 16, 19, 21).

method_links.note: Range reduction is in the definition, and all reduction switches are on by default. Probing, off by default in 2000 (S077), is now decided automatically. Preprocessor reduction also serves the multistart mode.
Every device has a numbered switch, so it can be ablated. The bibliography is declared to describe the implemented algorithms. The log prints the version, the build and the paper to cite.

LP/MIP relaxations with outer approximation; MIP relaxations take most of the time on integer problems. NLP local solvers are switched by problem characteristics and solver performance, and CPLEX falls back to CLP/CBC.

AllowFilterSD defaults to 0 for local search, while the sample log lists FILTERSD among the subsolvers the run may use. This manual does not settle what the 2022.1.19 note switching FilterSD off by default changed.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: version, build and the paper to cite in every run log
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The BARON 17.4.1 log header prints the version and build date and asks users to cite Tawarmalani and Sahinidis 2005. The ALAMO 2016.2.23 banner does the same (S249 pp. 78-79).

transferable: Give every reduction or relaxation device an integer switch with a documented default (off, on, automatic), so users and reviewers can run the ablation themselves (pp. 23-24).
Pair each termination status with what it certifies and what the user must change, and say outright when the printed bounds may be invalid (pp. 12-13).
In the option table, flag any option that makes runs nondeterministic, and state which clock enforces the time limit (pp. 21-22).
Offer a labelled heuristic mode of the global solver (multistart, iterations set to 0), so users do not stop the search early and read the incumbent as global (p. 18).
coauthors: none (sole author line, The Optimization Firm)

quotes.text: Even though relaxation bounds are printed on the screen to give the user a feeling for convergence, these bounds may not be valid for the problem at hand.
Because it relies on CPU time measurements, which may depend on machine load, this option may result in nondeterministic behavior.

title: The Center for Advanced Process Decision-making at Carnegie Mellon
contribution: A column by the three CAPD directors describing the CMU process-systems consortium (more than 20 companies, five faculty, more than 70 students and researchers, a short course since 1988), whose engine is member-supplied case studies and software.
problem_entry: n/a (institutional column in the ChE lifelong learning series) (p. 1).
key_idea: n/a: the consortium's structure, the EWO and ESI interest groups, and member benefits (reports, papers, software, an annual review, the short course) (pp. 1-4).
positioning: n/a (no literature). His 2007 arrival is credited with strengths in core optimization and with molecular-level applications (p. 2).
writing: Institutional and promotional: one Dow success story with multimillion-dollar savings, and short-course testimonials (pp. 3-4).
limits_future: No limits are named. The outlook is leading-edge fundamental research applied to real-world problems, with education as the key mission (p. 5).

method_links.note: Weak (center level, in the three authors' voice): software tools are adopted in free and commercial forms, software is delivered to members, and lecture material and software link teaching back to research.

quotes.text: These companies typically supply case-study projects that are undertaken by PSE faculty and students.

we have found that there exists a strong interplay between research and teaching that results in the development of high quality educational materials, including lecture material and software that, in turn, catalyze further research advances.

title: Mixed-integer nonlinear programming 2018
contribution: A sole-authored editorial opening the OPTE special issue on MINLP 2018. It gives a short history of MINLP and summarizes ten papers, five of which report beating BARON with tailored methods. It notes that over 20 general-purpose MINLP solvers are now reported.
problem_entry: n/a (editorial): introduces the field and the issue, which grew out of Dagstuhl seminar 18081 (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: n/a: MINLP with algebraic, factorable functions; a history from LP to Beale and Forrest; chemical engineering as the natural home (Duran and Grossmann); six global codes listed (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Terminology: a problem is convex if dropping integrality leaves a convex model (p. 2).
experiments: none (relays the papers' claims: five of ten outperform BARON, four of them also SCIP, and in the 16-solver, 335-problem convex comparison SHOT edges out BARON; pp. 3-4)
positioning: Cites his own work at three points: BARON 1996, the Kılınç-Sahinidis review, and two BARON papers where BARON trails SHOT. Rivals' wins over BARON are reported without qualification (pp. 2-4).
writing: One paragraph per paper, each ending with its comparative result against named solvers. The conclusion counts the recurring themes, networks and bilinear constraints (pp. 3-4).
limits_future: Forecasts advances from convexification, decomposition and parallel implementations, including for uncertainty and machine learning. Notes a one-year review cycle and OPTE's shift toward core theory and algorithms (p. 4).

method_links.note: Weak: he picks out the issue's large comparison (16 solvers, 335 problems, results analysed by nonlinearity and discreteness) as very thorough.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: rival wins over his own solver relayed without qualification
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Five of the ten papers summarized report outperforming BARON, and this is stated plainly. The conclusion says many tailored algorithms outperform general-purpose solvers.

transferable: In a special-issue editorial, end each paper's summary with its comparative result against named solvers, so the conclusion can count how often tailored methods beat general ones (pp. 3-4).

quotes.text: Many of the papers develop tailored algorithms that outperform general-purpose MINLP solvers.
This is a rather remarkable development in an area for which only a handful of solvers existed a decade ago.
